name: Awbrey Glen
label: Awbrey Glen
about_prose: Awbrey Glen sits on Awbrey Butte on the northwest side of Bend. The site includes outcroppings of lava rock and reddish basalt, and Brooks Resources Corporation, which developed the community, says it preserved as many trees as possible during construction and applied fire-conscious building practices throughout. Brooks Resources broke ground in 1992, and the 18-hole golf course designed by Gene Mason opened for play in 1993. The gated residential sections reached build-out in 2006, the same year ownership of the club transitioned to its members. David McLay Kidd, the architect behind Tetherow and Bandon Dunes, later reworked Mason's original design. The course now plays from around 5,400 yards up to 7,019 yards from the back tees across six sets of tees, with a course rating of 72.8 and a slope of 135, so the same 18 holes ask something very different of a first-time golfer than they do of someone playing from the tips.

The practice facility is built for people who take the game seriously and for kids who are just starting. It includes a dual-ended driving range, practice bunkers, and putting and pitching greens staffed by PGA professionals, plus The Loop, a five-hole, par-three course that the club describes as the only one of its kind in Central Oregon. The youth program runs through an Explorer group with year-round outdoor activities, and the head youth coach, Tim Fraley, holds the U.S. Kids Golf Foundation's Master Kids Coach certification, a distinction the club says makes him the only coach with that credential in Central Oregon. Nineteen, the club restaurant, serves lunch and dinner under chef Jake McPeck with Cascade Range views from the dining room, and it is open to the public, not just members.

Beyond the course, the amenities include a lap pool, a kiddie pool, and a hot tub open through the summer, plus a private catch-and-release lake stocked with rainbow trout. Give Back, a member-run nonprofit based at the club, has distributed more than $1 million to Central Oregon families in need. Mt. Bachelor is about 30 minutes southwest by way of Century Drive, roughly 22 miles from the community, which matters to a household that skis or rides as much as it golfs.

The Deschutes River Trail's Awbrey Reach segment, built over a buried Tumalo irrigation canal, terminates inside the Awbrey Glen neighborhood, according to Bend Park and Recreation District. It runs 3.9 miles round trip on compacted gravel, with views down into the Deschutes River canyon and across to Riley Ranch Nature Reserve, and it connects north to the Archie Briggs Canyon Trail by way of a steep climb. The trade-off is access. Most people reach the trail by parking at Sawyer Park first, since parking is very limited on the Awbrey Glen end, and the trail does not cross the river to Riley Ranch itself.

Living in Awbrey Glen means paying into two separate structures. The gated residential sections are run by a homeowners association, managed independently of the club. Club membership is a second, optional layer on top of that, with roughly 375 current members choosing among family, generational, golf, and sports membership options, and it is the club, not the HOA, that now owns the course and clubhouse. Guest access follows the same split: sponsored guests can play the golf course, but the pool, the practice facility, and the fishing lake are reserved for members only. That structure fits a buyer who wants the golf lifestyle and is willing to fund the club as well as the neighborhood. It is a poorer fit for someone who wants Awbrey Butte scenery without a club commitment, or who wants to walk out the front door onto a trail rather than drive to Sawyer Park to reach one.
